title: PII & Secrets Handling
summary: Agents pass text through models, logs, and traces you don't fully control, so anything sensitive that enters can leak out later. The discipline is twofold: detect and redact PII before it's sent or stored, and keep secrets out of prompts and logs entirely — inject credentials at the tool boundary, scope keys to the minimum, and set retention limits. A small redaction utility plus least-privilege key handling covers most of the real risk.
nestedConcepts: keep secrets out of prompts & logs

subtopics.title: PII and secrets are different risks
subtopics.explanation: PII is data about people — emails, phone numbers, national IDs — that you must minimize and protect for privacy and compliance reasons. Secrets are credentials — API keys, tokens, passwords — whose exposure directly grants access to systems. They call for different handling: PII you redact or mask so meaning survives without identity, while secrets you keep out of the model's context and logs altogether. Telling the two apart is what lets you apply the right control to each.
subtopics.example:
# PII: about a person -> redact/mask, keep the shape
email = "ada@example.com"        # -> '[EMAIL]' or 'a**@example.com'

# SECRET: a credential -> never put in prompt/log, inject at tool boundary
api_key = os.environ["PAYMENTS_API_KEY"]   # stays out of model context

# same string type, opposite handling: mask PII, hide secrets

subtopics.title: Detect and redact PII before it's sent or stored
subtopics.explanation: Before untrusted or user text goes into a prompt, a log line, or a trace, run it through a redactor that finds common PII patterns and replaces them with typed placeholders. Redacting early means the sensitive value never reaches the model provider or your log store, shrinking where a leak can originate. A reusable redaction utility is the single most practical PII control an agent can adopt.

subtopics.title: Keep secrets out of prompts and logs
subtopics.explanation: A credential should never appear in the model's context, in a prompt template, or in a log or trace — anywhere it lands, it can be exfiltrated by injection or leaked by an accidental dump. Instead, keep secrets in the environment or a vault and inject them only at the tool-execution boundary, where your code (not the model) uses them. Keeping secrets off the text path removes the most catastrophic single leak vector an agent has.
subtopics.example:
import os

# BAD: secret in the prompt -> visible to model + any log of the prompt
# prompt = f"Use key {os.environ['STRIPE_KEY']} to charge..."  # never do this

# GOOD: model names the tool; code supplies the secret at the boundary
def charge(amount: int, customer: str) -> str:
    key = os.environ["STRIPE_KEY"]        # read here, not in the prompt
    return f"charged {amount} to {customer}"   # key never enters context

subtopics.title: Scope keys to least privilege
subtopics.explanation: Every credential an agent can reach should grant the narrowest access that still lets the task succeed: read-only where writes aren't needed, a single resource rather than a whole account, and short-lived tokens over long-lived ones. Scoping limits the blast radius if a key does leak, turning a potential full compromise into a contained one. Least-privilege key handling is the assumption-of-breach counterpart to keeping secrets hidden.

subtopics.title: Set data-retention limits
subtopics.explanation: Decide up front how long prompts, outputs, and traces that might contain sensitive data are kept, and delete them on schedule; also prefer providers/settings that don't retain your data for training. Short retention means that even a store you forgot to lock down holds less, for less time. Bounding retention is the final layer that limits how much sensitive history an incident could ever expose.
subtopics.example:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

RETENTION = timedelta(days=30)

def purge_expired(records: list[dict], now=None) -> list[dict]:
    now = now or datetime.utcnow()
    # drop anything older than the retention window
    return [r for r in records if now - r["created"] < RETENTION]
# short windows shrink how much sensitive data any leak can expose

foundations.overview: An agent moves text through components you don't fully control — a model provider, log aggregators, tracing systems — so any sensitive value that enters that path can surface later in a place you didn't intend. Managing this splits cleanly into two disciplines. For PII (data about people: emails, phone numbers, IDs), the control is detect-and-redact: run user or untrusted text through a redactor that replaces recognized patterns with typed placeholders before it reaches a prompt, log, or trace, so the raw value never leaves your boundary. For secrets (credentials: API keys, tokens), the control is stronger — keep them out of the model's context and logs entirely, inject them only at the tool-execution boundary where your code uses them, scope each key to the least privilege the task needs, and prefer short-lived tokens. Wrapping both is data retention: decide how long prompts, outputs, and traces are kept, delete on schedule, and avoid providers that retain your data. None of these is exotic — a small reusable redaction utility plus least-privilege, boundary-injected secrets and bounded retention together neutralize the large majority of real-world leak risk for an agent.
foundations.formalDefinition: PII handling is the detection and redaction or masking of personally identifiable information before it is transmitted to a model or written to logs/traces. Secrets handling is the practice of excluding credentials from prompts, logs, and model context, injecting them only at the tool-execution boundary, scoping them to least privilege, and preferring short-lived tokens. Data retention is the policy bounding how long sensitive prompts, outputs, and traces are stored before deletion.
foundations.whyItMatters: Agents multiply the surfaces where data lands — provider APIs, prompt logs, distributed traces — and prompt injection can actively try to exfiltrate whatever is in context. Redacting PII and keeping secrets off the text path directly reduce both accidental leaks and injection-driven exfiltration, which is a hard requirement under privacy regulation and enterprise security review.
foundations.mentalModel: Treat the agent's context and logs like a postcard: assume anyone along the route can read it. You'd never write your bank PIN on a postcard, so secrets never go in the text — you hand them over in a sealed envelope (the tool boundary) only when needed. Personal details on the postcard you black out with a marker (redaction) before mailing, and you shred your copies after a set time (retention).
foundations.realWorldUsage: Redaction utilities run on inbound user messages and retrieved documents before prompting and before logging; secrets live in environment variables or a vault and are read inside tool functions, never templated into prompts; keys are minted read-only or single-resource and short-lived; and pipelines apply TTL-based deletion to conversation and trace stores. Providers are configured for zero data retention where available.
foundations.performanceImpact: Redaction is a lightweight regex/scan pass with negligible cost next to a model call, and it can reduce token count by shortening long PII spans. Reading secrets from the environment at the tool boundary adds nothing measurable, and short-lived scoped tokens have only occasional refresh overhead.
commonUseCases: Redacting PII from user input and retrieved docs before prompting/logging
Injecting API keys at the tool boundary instead of in prompts
Minting least-privilege, short-lived credentials per task
Applying retention TTLs to conversation and trace stores

commonMisconceptions.myth: It's fine to put an API key in the system prompt if the prompt is 'hidden'.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The prompt is visible to the model and lands in logs and traces; injection can exfiltrate it. Secrets must stay out of context and be injected at the tool boundary.

commonMisconceptions.myth: PII redaction and secret handling are the same task.
commonMisconceptions.reality: PII is masked so meaning survives without identity; secrets are removed from the text path entirely. Same-looking strings, opposite controls.

commonMisconceptions.myth: If data is only in temporary logs, retention doesn't matter.
commonMisconceptions.reality: 'Temporary' logs are copied into aggregators and traces that persist; without an explicit retention/deletion policy, sensitive data accumulates and widens any breach.

interactiveExamples.title: A reusable PII redaction utility
interactiveExamples.explanation: Redact common PII into typed placeholders before text reaches a prompt or a log. Typed placeholders keep the text readable and structure-preserving while removing the identifying value.

code.code:
import re

# ordered so more specific patterns run first
PATTERNS = [
    ("EMAIL", re.compile(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+")),
    ("PHONE", re.compile(r"\b\d{3}[-.\s]?\d{3}[-.\s]?\d{4}\b")),
    ("CARD",  re.compile(r"\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,16}\b")),
]

def redact_pii(text: str) -> str:
    for label, rx in PATTERNS:
        text = rx.sub(f"[{label}]", text)   # replace value with its type
    return text

msg = "Reach Ada at ada@example.com or 555-123-4567."
print(redact_pii(msg))
code.caption: The email and phone number become typed placeholders, so the sentence stays meaningful but carries no identifying value into the prompt or log.

interactiveExamples.title: Secrets at the tool boundary, redaction on the log path
interactiveExamples.explanation: Keep the credential out of the model's context by reading it inside the tool, and route every log line through the redactor so PII and any stray secret-shaped token never persist. This combines least-exposure secret handling with defensive logging.

code.code:
import os, re, logging

log = logging.getLogger("agent")

_SECRET = re.compile(r"(?i)(api[_-]?key|token|secret)\s*[:=]\s*\S+")
_EMAIL = re.compile(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+")

def safe_log(msg: str) -> str:
    msg = _SECRET.sub(r"\1=[REDACTED]", msg)   # strip credential-looking tokens
    msg = _EMAIL.sub("[EMAIL]", msg)            # strip PII
    return msg

def charge_customer(amount: int, email: str) -> str:
    # secret is read HERE, never placed in the prompt or returned text
    key = os.environ.get("PAYMENTS_API_KEY", "env-key")
    assert key                                  # used by code, not the model
    return f"charged {amount} to {email}"

result = charge_customer(2000, "ada@example.com")
print(safe_log(f"tool result: {result} api_key=sk_live_123"))
code.caption: The secret is used inside the tool and never enters the model context; the log line is redacted so neither the email nor the stray key persists.

codeLab.title: Build a redactor for logs and prompts
codeLab.instructions: Implement redact(text: str) -> str that replaces (1) email addresses with '[EMAIL]', (2) US-style phone numbers (e.g. 555-123-4567 or 555.123.4567) with '[PHONE]', and (3) any 'key=<value>', 'token=<value>', or 'secret=<value>' assignment (case-insensitive, with optional spaces around '=') with the same key name followed by '=[REDACTED]' (e.g. 'API_KEY=sk_live_9' -> 'API_KEY=[REDACTED]'). The function must be safe to call on any string and leave non-matching text unchanged. Complete it so the harness passes.

starter.code:
import re

def redact(text: str) -> str:
    # TODO: replace emails -> [EMAIL], phones -> [PHONE],
    # and key/token/secret assignments -> <name>=[REDACTED].
    # Leave everything else unchanged.
    ...

solution.code:
import re

EMAIL = re.compile(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+")
PHONE = re.compile(r"\b\d{3}[-.]\d{3}[-.]\d{4}\b")
# capture the credential's name so we can keep it and redact only the value
SECRET = re.compile(r"(?i)\b([\w-]*(?:key|token|secret))\s*=\s*\S+")

def redact(text: str) -> str:
    text = EMAIL.sub("[EMAIL]", text)                 # PII: email
    text = PHONE.sub("[PHONE]", text)                 # PII: phone
    # keep the field name, blank the value
    text = SECRET.sub(lambda m: f"{m.group(1)}=[REDACTED]", text)
    return text

codeLab.testHarness:
assert redact("mail ada@example.com") == "mail [EMAIL]"
assert redact("call 555-123-4567") == "call [PHONE]"
assert redact("call 555.123.4567") == "call [PHONE]"
assert redact("API_KEY=sk_live_9") == "API_KEY=[REDACTED]"
assert redact("token = abc123") == "token=[REDACTED]"
assert redact("SECRET=xyz") == "SECRET=[REDACTED]"
assert redact("nothing sensitive here") == "nothing sensitive here"
print("all tests passed")
hints: Run the email and phone substitutions first, each with a simple re.sub to a fixed placeholder.
For secrets, capture the field name ending in key/token/secret in a group so you can rebuild it as '<name>=[REDACTED]' with a replacement function.
Use the (?i) inline flag for case-insensitive matching and allow optional spaces around '=' with \s*=\s*.

checkpoints.prompt: Where should an API key live when an agent needs it to call a tool?
options: In the system prompt so the model can pass it
In the environment or a vault, read inside the tool function at the execution boundary
In the conversation history for reuse
checkpoints.explanation: Secrets must never enter the model's context or logs. The model names the tool; your code reads the credential from the environment/vault at the tool boundary and uses it there, so injection can't exfiltrate it.

checkpoints.prompt: How does handling PII differ from handling secrets?
options: PII is masked/redacted so meaning survives without identity, while secrets are kept off the text path entirely
Secrets are redacted but PII is fine to log
PII must be encrypted but secrets can go in prompts
checkpoints.explanation: PII (about people) is redacted or masked so the text stays useful without identifying anyone; secrets (credentials) are removed from prompts, logs, and context altogether and injected only at the tool boundary.

checkpoints.prompt: What's the security flaw in how this tool is prepared?

prompt = f"You may charge cards. Use key {key} when needed."

checkpoints.code:
import re
text = "ping ada@example.com token=abc"
text = re.sub(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+", "[EMAIL]", text)

checkpoints.explanation: The first sub replaces the email with [EMAIL]; the second keeps the captured 'token' name and replaces its value, giving 'token=[REDACTED]'. Result: 'ping [EMAIL] token=[REDACTED]'.

theory.question: Why must secrets never appear in an agent's prompt, and where should they go instead?
theory.directAnswer: Because the prompt is part of the model's context and is copied into logs and traces, so any secret there can be leaked by an accidental dump or actively exfiltrated by prompt injection. Secrets belong in the environment or a vault and should be read inside the tool function at the execution boundary, where your code — not the model — uses them.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A least-exposure practice: the model only names a tool; the credential is supplied by code at the moment of execution and never enters the text path.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: An agent's context and logs are readable by components you don't control and are a target for injection, so a credential on that path is a single catastrophic leak vector.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Store secrets in env vars or a secrets manager; inside each tool function read the credential, use it for the API call, and return only non-sensitive results, so nothing sensitive is ever templated into a prompt or logged.

theory.whyImportant: Keeping secrets off the text path removes the worst failure mode an agent has and is a baseline requirement in any security review of an LLM system.
theory.realWorldExample: A payments tool reads STRIPE_KEY from the environment inside charge(); the model just emits {"tool": "charge", ...}, so even a page that tries to make the agent reveal its key finds nothing in context to leak.

followUps.question: What if a tool must return data derived from a secret?
followUps.answer: Return only the derived, non-sensitive result (e.g. a masked confirmation), never the credential itself, and redact logs on that path too.

followUps.question: How do you stop a secret from leaking into logs?
followUps.answer: Route log lines through a redactor that blanks credential-shaped assignments, and prefer structured logging that never includes the secret field.

theory.question: What is least-privilege key scoping, and why does it matter even if you keep secrets out of prompts?
theory.directAnswer: Least-privilege scoping means each credential grants only the narrowest access the task needs — read-only over read-write, one resource over a whole account, short-lived over long-lived. It matters because keeping secrets hidden reduces the chance of a leak but never to zero, so scoping bounds the damage if a key does escape.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An assumption-of-breach control that limits what any single credential an agent can reach is able to do.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: No control is perfect; a scoped, short-lived key turns a potential full-account compromise into a contained, time-boxed one.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Mint task-specific credentials with minimal scopes and short TTLs, choose the right one per task, and let them expire quickly so a leaked token is both limited in power and useless soon after.

theory.whyImportant: It is the second half of secret safety: hiding secrets lowers leak probability, scoping lowers leak impact, and together they define a defensible posture.
theory.realWorldExample: A reporting agent uses a 'reports:read' token, so even if that token leaked it couldn't issue refunds or change data — the refund flow uses a separate, short-lived 'payments:refund' credential.

followUps.question: Why prefer short-lived tokens?
followUps.answer: A leaked short-lived token expires quickly, shrinking the window an attacker can use it, unlike a long-lived key that stays valid indefinitely.

followUps.question: How does scoping interact with tool allow-lists?
followUps.answer: They reinforce each other: allow-lists limit which tools run, scoping limits what those tools' credentials can do — defense-in-depth on both dimensions.

scenario.question: A review finds customer emails and one API key showing up in your agent's request logs. How would you fix the leak and prevent recurrence?
scenario.directAnswer: Stop the bleeding by rotating the exposed key and purging affected logs, then route all log/trace writes through a redactor that masks PII and blanks credential-shaped tokens, move the secret out of the prompt to a tool-boundary read, scope the new key to least privilege, and set a short retention TTL on the log store so old sensitive data is deleted automatically.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A leak-remediation and prevention problem spanning secrets in context, PII in logs, and unbounded retention.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The key was likely templated into a prompt that got logged, and user text with emails was logged verbatim, while no retention policy limited how long either persisted.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Rotate and re-scope the credential, add a redaction pass (email/phone -> placeholders, key/token/secret assignments -> [REDACTED]) on the logging and prompting paths, read the secret inside the tool instead of the prompt, and apply TTL-based purging to conversation and trace stores.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows the full lifecycle — contain, redact, re-architect the secret path, scope, and bound retention — rather than a one-off patch, which is exactly what a security review expects.
scenario.realWorldExample: After rotating the key and adding a redactor to the logging middleware plus a 30-day retention purge, subsequent logs showed '[EMAIL]' and 'api_key=[REDACTED]' and the sensitive backlog aged out automatically.

followUps.question: Why rotate the key even after redacting logs?
followUps.answer: Once a secret has been exposed it must be treated as compromised; redaction prevents future leaks but can't un-expose the value already written.

followUps.question: How do you verify redaction actually works?
followUps.answer: Add tests asserting known PII and secret patterns are masked, and periodically scan a sample of logs for unredacted patterns as a regression check.

coding.question: Write a redact(text) utility that masks emails and phone numbers and blanks the value of any key/token/secret assignment, leaving other text unchanged, suitable for both prompts and logs.
coding.thoughtProcess: I want one pass that handles the two PII types with fixed placeholders and one pass for credential assignments where I must keep the field name but drop the value. For the credential case I capture the name ending in key/token/secret in a group and use a replacement function so 'API_KEY=sk_9' becomes 'API_KEY=[REDACTED]'. I use case-insensitive matching and allow optional spaces around '=', and I make sure non-matching text is untouched.

solution.code:
import re

EMAIL = re.compile(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+")
PHONE = re.compile(r"\b\d{3}[-.]\d{3}[-.]\d{4}\b")
# capture the credential name so we keep it and blank only its value
SECRET = re.compile(r"(?i)\b([\w-]*(?:key|token|secret))\s*=\s*\S+")

def redact(text: str) -> str:
    text = EMAIL.sub("[EMAIL]", text)      # PII: email -> placeholder
    text = PHONE.sub("[PHONE]", text)      # PII: phone -> placeholder
    text = SECRET.sub(lambda m: f"{m.group(1)}=[REDACTED]", text)
    return text

if __name__ == "__main__":
    line = "user ada@example.com called 555-123-4567 with API_KEY=sk_live_9"
    print(redact(line))

lineByLine: EMAIL matches typical addresses and is replaced wholesale with the typed placeholder [EMAIL].
PHONE matches US-style 3-3-4 numbers separated by '-' or '.' and becomes [PHONE].
SECRET captures a field name ending in key/token/secret (group 1) followed by '=' and a value.
The replacement function rebuilds '<name>=[REDACTED]', preserving the field name while removing the sensitive value.
The (?i) flag makes the credential match case-insensitive and \s*=\s* tolerates spaces around '='.
The __main__ block shows one line with all three redactions applied at once.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) in the length of the text for each regex pass, O(n) overall.

followUps.question: How would you avoid redacting a legitimate value that just looks like a phone number?
followUps.answer: Tighten the pattern with context or word boundaries, or use a dedicated PII library with validation; accept that redaction favors false positives (over-masking) for safety.

followUps.question: Where should redact() be called in an agent?
followUps.answer: On inbound user text and retrieved documents before prompting, and on every log/trace write, so sensitive values never reach the provider or the log store.

keyTakeaways: Agents pass text through models, logs, and traces you don't fully control, so anything sensitive that enters can leak later.
PII (about people) is detected and redacted/masked so meaning survives without identity — a small reusable redactor is the key control.
Secrets (credentials) must stay out of prompts, logs, and context entirely; inject them at the tool-execution boundary where code, not the model, uses them.
Scope every key to least privilege — read-only, single-resource, short-lived — so a leak is contained rather than catastrophic.
Bound data retention: delete prompts, outputs, and traces on a schedule and prefer no-retention providers so incidents expose as little as possible.
